newsitem.title: USA: Dole courts Christian group after convention snub.
newsitem.headline: Dole courts Christian group after convention snub.

text.p: Bob Dole, who gave short shrift to the Christian right at the Republican convention, appeared on Saturday before the Christian Coalition and asked for its support in his presidential campaign.

"I would ask you for your full and complete support every day, every day between now and November 5, 1996, when we will have a new president-elect," Dole told a cheering throng of nearly 5,000 at the coalition's convention.
"I can't tell you how much your support and encouragement and prayers mean to all of us," Dole said. "We understand your commitment, we understand your strength, we understand your potential."
Dole's appearance before the group was the result of a last-minute change in schedule, but it gave him a large and supportive audience in a group that had been cool to his two presidential opponents.

The crowd erupted in applause when coalition founder Pat Robertson, a one-time Dole opponent in the 1988 Republican presidential primaries, made a surprise introduction of Dole, called him a "dear friend" and raised joined hands with the Republican candidate at the podium.
"Jimminy," said Dole in response to the reaction.
Criticising Democratic U.S. President Bill Clinton for declining an invitation to speak, Robertson said, "I would ask, is there no room for any evangelicals in the Democratic Party?"
On Friday, the group had booed independent candidate Ross Perot when he said some believed his candidacy in 1992 helped bring Clinton to power.
The coalition and its executive director, Ralph Reed, were instrumental in giving Dole the credibility with the Republican Party's conservative wing necessary to win the nomination.
But, after a failed struggle to get the Republican Party's anti-abortion plank to include language that it was tolerant of differing views on the issue, Dole had kept his distance from the group.
Dole said he had not read the adopted platform, and pro-abortion voices were not on the agenda at the party's convention in San Diego.

But in citing a Biblical passage on Saturday regarding spirituality, Dole also evoked the importance of Christian activists to the Republican Party and his own struggling campaign, where he trails far behind Clinton in the polls.
"We certainly need strength beyond our own," Dole said.
The purpose of Dole's appearance was ostensibly to introduce his running mate, Jack Kemp, who previously had been scheduled to speak.

But Dole also ran through many of the themes of his campaign stump speech -- beginning with plugging his economic programme. He drew the loudest applause in calling for giving parents more choice in schools for their children, fighting drugs and crime, and condemning Clinton's veto of a bill to ban a rare late-term abortion procedure.
"When I get the partial birth abortion bill, I'll sign it. I won't veto it, I'll sign it," Dole said.
The Clinton-Gore campaign team took note of Dole's surprise appearance before the group.
"Watching Bob Dole arm in arm with Pat Robertson speaks volumes to the extreme agenda being pursued by the Dole/Kemp/Gingrich team," spokesman Joe Lockhart said in a statement.

"We now know who's in charge of the Dole/Kemp team. First, the Kemp nomination was held up waiting for Pat Robertson's personal approval. Now, after weeks of telling the Christian Coalition he could not attend their meeting, Bob Dole just happened to show up after Robertson said it would take 'a miracle from Almighty God' to win this election."
